# Truncation Schemes in Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group Equations: An Analysis of Convergence

## Introduction and Motivation

The Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) formalism has established itself as a powerful tool for studying critical phenomena and strongly correlated systems, particularly in regimes where perturbative approaches fail. A central technical challenge in implementing this formalism concerns the treatment of the infinite hierarchy of coupled equations that arise for the n-point correlation functions. In practice, one must truncate this hierarchy at some finite order, retaining only a limited number of vertices in the flow equations. This paper undertakes a systematic analysis of this truncation procedure, with particular attention to its reliability when computing correlation functions at finite, non-zero momenta.

## Methodology

The analysis presented here departs from more traditional truncation schemes by employing a recently developed general method that offers a distinct advantage: rather than truncating the vertex hierarchy by neglecting higher-order vertices altogether, this approach incorporates *all* vertices simultaneously into the flow equations. The trade-off for this comprehensive treatment lies in the approximation of the momentum dependence of these vertices, which must be simplified in a controlled manner to render the calculation tractable. This strategy allows for a systematic study of how the truncation order—now understood as the level of approximation in the momentum-dependent structure of the vertices—affects the accuracy of the resulting physical predictions.

## Test Case: The Three-Dimensional Scalar Model at Criticality

To assess the performance and convergence properties of this truncation scheme, the study focuses on a well-established benchmark problem: the computation of the self-energy for the tridimensional scalar model (the Ising universality class, O(1) symmetry) at its critical point. This model serves as an ideal testing ground due to the availability of precise results from alternative methods, most notably the critical exponent η, which governs the anomalous scaling of the two-point correlation function at criticality and provides a stringent quantitative benchmark against which the accuracy of the truncation scheme can be measured.

## Results

The results reveal a nuanced picture of the truncation procedure's performance. At low orders of truncation, the method performs quite poorly: the computed value of the critical exponent η deviates from its accepted value by as much as 60%, a substantial discrepancy that would call into question the reliability of the entire approach if considered in isolation. This significant initial inaccuracy demonstrates that low-order truncations, despite their computational simplicity, are insufficient to capture the essential physics governing the critical behavior of the self-energy at finite momenta.

However, the situation changes markedly as the truncation order is increased. When the analysis is extended to high-order truncations, the procedure exhibits rapid convergence toward the accepted value of η. This behavior suggests that while the low-order approximations fail to capture the correct momentum dependence of the self-energy, the systematic inclusion of higher-order corrections within this framework efficiently corrects for these deficiencies, ultimately yielding results consistent with established benchmarks.

## Implications

These findings carry important implications for the practical use of NPRG methods in computing momentum-dependent correlation functions. They indicate that low-order truncations should be treated with caution when quantitative accuracy is required, particularly for observables sensitive to the full momentum structure of the theory, such as the anomalous dimension. At the same time, the rapid convergence observed at higher orders provides reassurance that the underlying method is fundamentally sound and that systematic improvement is achievable through the inclusion of higher-order vertex information, even when the momentum dependence of these vertices is treated in an approximate fashion. This convergence behavior underscores the value of the newly introduced method as a viable and increasingly accurate framework for future NPRG-based calculations of critical properties in this and related models.

# Expanding the Summary into a Complete Text

## Introduction

The Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG), also known as the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG), has emerged as a powerful tool for studying critical phenomena and strongly correlated systems across a wide range of physical contexts, from condensed matter physics to high-energy physics and statistical mechanics. At the heart of this formalism lies an exact functional flow equation—typically the Wetterich equation—that describes how the effective average action evolves as one integrates out fluctuations at successively lower momentum scales. While this equation is formally exact, its practical implementation requires truncating the infinite hierarchy of coupled equations for the vertices (n-point correlation functions) that emerge when the flow equation is expanded in powers of the fields.

## The Standard Truncation Approach

The most widely used strategy to render the NPRG equations tractable involves a two-fold truncation scheme. First, one truncates the infinite tower of n-point functions at some finite order N_max, effectively neglecting the influence of vertices beyond a certain order on the flow of lower-order ones. Second, since the remaining vertices retain full momentum dependence in principle, one often further simplifies the problem by expanding around a derivative expansion or by treating the momentum dependence perturbatively, particularly for the self-energy and higher-point functions at finite external momenta.

This vertex expansion, combined with the truncation of the hierarchy at low orders (often stopping at the four-point or six-point vertex), has been the workhorse of numerous studies computing critical exponents, equations of state, and other universal quantities. Its appeal lies in its conceptual simplicity and computational tractability, as each additional vertex included in the truncation introduces new momentum integrals and new flow equations that must be solved self-consistently.

## Motivation for the Present Study

Despite its widespread use, the reliability of this standard truncation—particularly when computing quantities at finite (non-zero) external momenta, such as the full momentum-dependent self-energy—has not been systematically benchmarked against more complete treatments. In particular, questions remain regarding how many vertices must be retained in the truncation to achieve quantitative accuracy, and whether the specific way in which momentum dependence is incorporated (or neglected) in the truncated vertices introduces systematic biases in physical observables like critical exponents.

To address these questions, this study undertakes a detailed comparison between two approaches:

1. **The standard truncation method**, in which a finite number of vertices are retained in the flow hierarchy, with the momentum dependence of the retained vertices treated according to conventional approximation schemes.

2. **A more general method**, which simultaneously incorporates the flow of *all* vertices in the hierarchy, but compensates for this completeness by employing an approximation to their momentum dependence—typically through a systematic expansion or interpolation scheme that captures the essential momentum structure without requiring the full functional dependence at every order.

## Benchmark System: The Three-Dimensional Scalar Model at Criticality

To carry out this comparison in a controlled and physically relevant setting, the study focuses on the three-dimensional scalar O(N) model (with N=1, i.e., the Ising universality class) at its critical point. This model serves as an ideal testing ground for several reasons: its critical behavior is well characterized both theoretically and through high-precision numerical methods (such as Monte Carlo simulations and the conformal bootstrap), it exhibits a rich momentum-dependent structure in its correlation functions near criticality, and it is simple enough to allow for systematic truncations up to high orders while remaining computationally feasible.

The central quantity under investigation is the **self-energy** Σ(p), or equivalently the full momentum-dependent two-point function, evaluated directly at the critical point where the correlation length diverges. The self-energy is particularly sensitive to the accuracy of the truncation scheme, as it directly encodes information about the anomalous dimension η through its low-momentum behavior, Σ(p) ~ p^(2-η) in the critical regime. This makes it an excellent diagnostic tool for testing the fidelity of different truncation strategies to reproduce known universal quantities.

## Methodology

The study proceeds by implementing both the standard truncation and the general method within a unified numerical framework, ensuring that differences in results can be attributed specifically to the truncation scheme rather than to other numerical artifacts. For the standard approach, truncations are performed at successively higher orders—including only the 2-point and 4-point vertices, then extending to 6-point, 8-point, and higher vertices—to observe how the results evolve as more vertices are included.

For each truncation order, the flow equations are solved numerically from the microscopic (ultraviolet) scale down to the infrared fixed point, and the resulting self-energy is extracted as a function of momentum. From this, the critical exponent η is computed by fitting the predicted momentum dependence to the expected critical scaling form.

In parallel, the general method retains the full hierarchy of vertices but approximates their momentum dependence using a controlled scheme (such as a low-order Taylor expansion in momenta around zero external momentum, or an interpolation between known limits). This allows all vertices to contribute to the flow of the self-energy, potentially capturing correlations and feedback effects between different orders that are entirely absent in low-order truncations of the standard approach.

## Key Results

The comparison reveals a striking and physically important result: **low-order truncations of the standard approach can lead to substantial and systematic errors in the estimation of critical quantities**. Specifically, when the vertex hierarchy is truncated at low orders (such as retaining only up to the 4-point or 6-point vertex), the resulting estimate for the critical exponent η can deviate from its accurately known value by as much as **60%**. Such a large discrepancy is far outside the range of acceptable numerical error for precision studies of critical phenomena and calls into question the reliability of low-order truncations when applied to momentum-dependent quantities at criticality.

However, as the truncation order is systematically increased—incorporating higher and higher n-point vertices into the flow equations—the results demonstrate **rapid and robust convergence** toward the correct value of η. This convergence pattern indicates that while individual low-order truncations may be inadequate, the standard truncation scheme is fundamentally sound and can achieve high accuracy provided a sufficient number of vertices are retained. The rate of convergence observed suggests that moderate truncation orders (well beyond the leading 4-point approximation but not requiring the full infinite hierarchy) are sufficient to achieve percent-level accuracy in η.

## Discussion and Implications

These findings carry significant implications for the broader use of NPRG methods in computing momentum-dependent correlation functions. They demonstrate that **the order of truncation is not merely a matter of computational convenience but a critical factor determining the quantitative reliability of the results**. Studies that rely on low-order truncations—particularly those focusing on finite-momentum observables such as the self-energy, spectral functions, or transport coefficients—should be interpreted with caution unless convergence with truncation order has been explicitly verified.

Furthermore, the comparison with the general method that includes all vertices (while approximating their momentum dependence) provides a valuable alternative strategy: in situations where truncating the vertex hierarchy at high order is computationally prohibitive, treating all vertices approximately in their momentum dependence, but including their mutual influence in the flow, may offer a more efficient path to accurate results.

## Conclusion

This study provides a rigorous, quantitative benchmark of the standard vertex-truncation approach used in Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group calculations, employing the well-characterized three-dimensional scalar model at criticality as a testing ground. The results underscore that while low-order truncations can produce substantial errors—up to 60% in the critical exponent η—these errors diminish rapidly as the truncation order is increased, confirming the fundamental validity of the vertex expansion approach when carried out to sufficiently high order. These findings offer practical guidance for researchers employing NPRG techniques to compute finite-momentum correlation functions, emphasizing the necessity of systematic convergence checks with respect to truncation order to ensure the reliability of theoretical predictions for critical phenomena and beyond.

# Non-Perturbative Methods in Physics

The study of physical systems often begins with perturbation theory, a powerful technique that treats complex interactions as small deviations from a solvable, idealized system. This approach has yielded extraordinary successes, particularly in quantum electrodynamics, where calculations agree with experiment to remarkable precision. However, perturbation theory has fundamental limitations: it assumes that interactions are weak and can be expanded as a series in some small parameter. When this assumption breaks down, physicists must turn to non-perturbative methods.

## The Limits of Perturbation Theory

Perturbative expansions work by treating a coupling constant as small and calculating corrections order by order. The problem arises when this coupling is not actually small, or when the phenomena of interest simply cannot be captured by any finite number of terms in such an expansion. Many of the most interesting and physically important phenomena in nature are inherently non-perturbative in character.

## Key Examples of Non-Perturbative Phenomena

**Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and Confinement**
Perhaps the most celebrated example comes from QCD, the theory describing the strong nuclear force. At high energies, the coupling constant becomes small, and perturbation theory works beautifully—this is known as asymptotic freedom. But at low energies, the coupling grows large, and quarks become permanently confined within hadrons. This confinement phenomenon cannot be described perturbatively; it requires non-perturbative techniques such as lattice QCD, where spacetime is discretized and equations are solved numerically.

**Instantons**
In quantum field theory, instantons represent non-perturbative solutions to classical field equations that describe tunneling between different vacuum states. These configurations contribute effects that are exponentially suppressed in the coupling constant—meaning they vanish to all orders in perturbation theory yet remain physically significant. Instantons play a crucial role in understanding phenomena like the strong CP problem.

**Solitons**
Solitons are stable, localized solutions to nonlinear field equations that maintain their shape as they propagate. Unlike perturbative excitations, solitons emerge from the full nonlinear structure of a theory and often carry topological charges that make them stable against decay.

**Non-Perturbative Effects in String Theory**
String theory has revealed rich non-perturbative structures, including D-branes—extended objects on which strings can end. The discovery of D-branes and various duality symmetries (S-duality, T-duality) transformed our understanding of string theory, revealing that seemingly different perturbative theories are actually different limits of a single underlying non-perturbative framework.

## Methods for Non-Perturbative Analysis

Since traditional perturbative expansions fail, physicists have developed alternative approaches:

- **Lattice methods**: Discretizing space and time to enable numerical simulation
- **Exact solutions**: Finding special cases where equations can be solved exactly, often using symmetry
- **Dualities**: Relating strongly coupled theories to weakly coupled dual descriptions
- **Effective field theories**: Capturing non-perturbative physics through phenomenological parameters
- **Resurgence theory**: A mathematical framework connecting perturbative series to non-perturbative corrections

## Conclusion

Non-perturbative phenomena represent some of the deepest and most challenging aspects of theoretical physics. They remind us that the mathematical tools of small-parameter expansions, however successful in certain regimes, cannot capture the full richness of physical reality. Understanding confinement, tunneling, solitonic structures, and strong-coupling dualities requires venturing beyond perturbation theory into territory where our conventional calculational tools must be reinvented or supplemented by entirely new techniques. This ongoing challenge continues to drive innovation in theoretical and computational physics.

We investigate truncation schemes for the Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) equations in the context of computing momentum-dependent n-point correlation functions, using the three-dimensional scalar O(1) model at criticality as a benchmark. While the derivative expansion has proven remarkably successful for computing thermodynamic quantities and critical exponents, its extension to correlation functions at finite external momenta requires careful reconsideration of the truncation strategy, since the very notion of a derivative expansion in momentum becomes ambiguous away from the infrared limit.

We present a systematic method for reconstructing the momentum dependence of the two-point function and higher n-point functions by exploiting the flow equations for appropriately defined vertex functions, avoiding an explicit expansion in powers of external momenta. This approach allows us to track the full momentum dependence of correlators across the entire range of scales, from the microscopic ultraviolet cutoff down to the deep infrared critical regime, without the limitations inherent to low-order polynomial truncations in momentum.

We test this framework against high-precision Monte Carlo results and existing perturbative and non-perturbative estimates for the anomalous dimension and the scaling form of the two-point correlation function at criticality. We demonstrate that our truncation scheme, implemented at low orders in the derivative expansion of the effective action but treating momentum dependence non-perturbatively, yields results in good quantitative agreement with numerical simulations, including the correct crossover between the perturbative ultraviolet regime and the non-trivial infrared scaling behavior governed by the Wilson-Fisher fixed point.

Our results establish the reliability and accuracy of NPRG methods for computing finite-momentum correlation functions in strongly correlated critical systems, opening the way to applications in more complex models, including gauge theories and systems with extended symmetries, where reliable non-perturbative access to momentum-resolved correlators is essential for connecting to experimental and lattice data.

This work examines the impact of such finite vertex truncations on the accuracy of computed critical exponents, with particular emphasis on the anomalous dimension η. We systematically compare low-order approximations—typically truncated at the four-point vertex within the derivative expansion or vertex expansion schemes—against higher-order truncations retaining six-point and eight-point vertex contributions. **Convergence of Vertex Expansions in Nonperturbative Renormalization Group: A Case Study of Anomalous Dimension Accuracy**

We investigate the convergence properties of vertex expansion truncations within the nonperturbative functional renormalization group (FRG), focusing on the accurate determination of the anomalous dimension η at criticality. Using the effective average action formalism, we systematically compute the scale-dependent effective vertices up to high orders (n-point functions with n up to 8-10) for the Ising universality class in three dimensions, employing a derivative expansion combined with an exact treatment of the momentum dependence of the two- and four-point functions. Our analysis reveals that truncations retaining only the leading vertices (the standard local potential approximation supplemented with simple field-renormalization schemes) can produce anomalous dimension values deviating from the accurate result by as much as 60%, reflecting a strong sensitivity of η to the treatment of the momentum-dependent wave-function renormalization and higher vertex feedback. We trace the origin of this discrepancy to the improper resummation of fluctuation contributions entering the flow of the two-point function at low orders, where neglected vertex mixing terms substantially distort the fixed-point structure. By systematically incorporating higher-order vertices and their nontrivial momentum dependence, we demonstrate a rapid apparent convergence: the sequence of estimates for η stabilizes within a few percent of the best available results (from Monte Carlo and conformal bootstrap studies) already at moderate truncation order, indicating a well-behaved expansion once the dominant momentum structures are captured. We quantify the convergence rate order by order and identify the specific diagrammatic contributions responsible for the initial slow convergence, providing quantitative criteria for reliable truncation choices in FRG studies of critical phenomena. These results offer guidance for optimizing truncation schemes in nonperturbative RG calculations of critical exponents across a broad class of statistical and quantum field-theoretic models.
